52.canonical: Separate business logic from hardware and platform: intermingling software and firmware is an anti-pattern (burying SQL or spreading platform dependencies is writing firmware), so firm the boundary with a Hardware Abstraction Layer whose API is tailored to the software and hides how the hardware works, layering the hardware at the bottom so an inevitable hardware change is not a bigger job than necessary.

80.canonical: Treat large-scale change as sociotechnical: changing technology (e.g. breaking up a monolith) is not enough on its own, so deliberately evolve organizational structure, processes, and culture alongside software and data, recognizing the architect's role now includes designing the organization.

82.canonical: Favour immutable, deterministically rederivable views over long-lived mutated databases: keep the immutable event log separate from mutable state and derive read-optimized views from it, so a new view can be built alongside existing ones and views recreated from the log when moving between environments instead of doing in-place migrations or copying database files.

89.canonical: Route messages that cannot be processed to a dedicated channel rather than blocking the flow: send messages a receiver cannot process (e.g. schema-valid but semantically invalid or unreadable) to an Invalid Message / error channel so processing continues and they can be reprocessed later, and rely on the platform's Dead Letter Channel for undeliverable messages.

105.canonical: Design distributed systems for network reality rather than as if they were a single in-process application: explicitly counter the fallacies of distributed computing — the network is unreliable (use timeouts/circuit breakers), latency is non-zero (track average and tail latency), bandwidth is finite (minimize data, avoid stamp coupling), the network is insecure (secure every endpoint), the topology changes, and platforms are heterogeneous.

108.canonical: Never treat a common data representation as common semantics: integrating heterogeneous systems brings semantic and conceptual dissonance where the same field means different things across divisions, so explicitly resolve semantic differences and plan reconciliation as a combined business and technical task rather than assuming shared meaning.

116.canonical: Design every Aggregator around three explicit decisions — correlation (by a unique per-transaction identifier rather than a shared attribute), a completeness condition, and an aggregation algorithm — keeping the aggregation logic in strongly-typed domain objects independent of the messaging API.

120.canonical: Use a Message Filter so each system receives only the messages matching its criteria, dropping unwanted messages from a channel; run it stateless for parallelism or stateful when it must remember history such as for de-duplication.

121.canonical: Prefer coarse-grained, self-contained remote interfaces over fine-grained ones — bundling work into fewer, bulkier calls to minimize round trips, synchronization overhead, and coupling — keeping this remote interface distinct from a fine-grained local interface, while balancing against interfaces so coarse they limit flexibility.

126.canonical: Use asynchronous, queue-based pipelines to raise throughput by decoupling producer and consumer: parallelize the slowest stage with Competing Consumers on a Point-to-Point Channel, parallelize only stateless filters, and preserve ordering when it is critical with a single instance, a Resequencer, or a correlation identifier to match out-of-order results.

127.canonical: Make production filters transactional so a failure before the output is sent does not lose the message: open a transaction before consuming the input and commit only after publishing the output, aborting on any exception to roll back both and return the input to the queue.

136.canonical: On a Publish-Subscribe Channel a subscriber only receives messages published while it is actively subscribed, so subscribe before messages of interest are published and use a Durable Subscriber when an observer must receive messages published while it was temporarily disconnected.

138.canonical: Make communication two-way with a pair of Request-Reply messages: have the requestor specify a Return Address in the request header so the replier need not hard-code channels, and carry a Correlation Identifier (set to the request's message ID) on the reply so the requestor can match each reply to its request.

167.canonical: Map between domain objects and messages with a separate Messaging Mapper that neither the domain objects nor the messaging infrastructure know about (messages carry only scalar data, not references or inheritance), since embedding mapping in the domain object couples it to messaging and blocks reuse; invoke it through events, reduce its boilerplate with reflection or code generation, and pair it with a Message Translator that handles structural mapping to the Canonical Data Model.

192.canonical: Define architecture characteristics as objective, measurable values: decompose composite characteristics (such as agility) into measurable contributors, measure maxima not just averages, set budgets grounded in statistics, and treat unmeasurability as a sign of a vague definition.

195.canonical: Make architecture governance an automated, continuous responsibility: codify governance rules as fitness functions / automated architecture tests (e.g. ArchUnit, NetArchTest) built into the CI pipeline rather than relying on error-prone manual reviews, so important-but-not-urgent concerns like cyclic dependencies are caught automatically.

196.canonical: Adopt chaos engineering: treat failure as a matter of when not if, and deliberately inject faults into the running system in a controlled, monitored way (for example randomly killing processes, as with Chaos Monkey) to continually exercise the recovery machinery and build confidence that real faults are handled, especially where emergent behavior makes full testing impossible.

201.canonical: Use the 'does it require domain knowledge?' litmus test to separate architecture characteristics from domain criteria: an architecture characteristic is abstract and reusable across applications, whereas anything needing domain knowledge to interpret belongs to the domain — so validate characteristics with fitness functions and validate domain criteria with unit and functional tests.

220.canonical: Record every meaningful architecture decision as an Architecture Decision Record capturing Context (problem and alternatives), Decision (stated affirmatively, with its justification and emphasizing why over how), and Consequences (impacts and trade-offs considered), plus governance/compliance; keep each ADR as its own linked record and use an RFC-with-deadline to avoid analysis paralysis.

231.canonical: Treat meetings as costly synchronization points and protect the team's focus time: avoid meetings as the default interaction, control the ones you call (qualify invites with a why and agenda, distribute material beforehand, attend only the relevant parts), avoid standing status meetings, and respect developer flow.

251.canonical: Match each tool to the problem rather than defaulting to the tool already at hand: define the size and scope of the problem before building a solution, pick the smallest set of tools you can, and recognize that a tool built for a different kind of application can hinder more than help.

253.canonical: Prefer a web/HTML browser presentation and adopt a rich client only when you must, because web front ends avoid client-deployment problems and are increasingly capable; treat presentation as relatively independent of the lower layers, with Model-View-Controller underneath, and choose controllers and views (Page vs Front Controller, Template vs Transform View) by the site's nature and team tooling.

255.canonical: Keep all classes in a single process and do not separate layers into distinct processes unless you absolutely must, because distribution degrades performance and forces extra patterns like Remote Facade and Data Transfer Object; to use multiple processors, prefer clustering — run multiple copies of the single-process application across nodes so every call stays local and fine-grained.

266.canonical: Minimize database round-trips when reading: pull back multiple rows at once and load related tables with a single multitable join rather than issuing repeated or per-association queries (the N+1 problem, e.g. 101 queries for 100 employees and their skills), checking the Identity Map first so an already-loaded object is reused; because the join optimization is awkward and joins degrade past about three or four per query, apply it where the queries are slow and important.

267.canonical: Prefer separate finder objects over static find methods so database operations stay polymorphic and substitutable (for example replaceable by a Service Stub in tests or across different data sources), and run queries at the start of a unit of work since finders see committed database state, not unsaved in-memory objects.

281.canonical: Add an Application Controller only when the machine controls screen flow — there are definite rules about the order pages are visited and state-dependent view choices — and skip it when the user is free to reach any screen in any order; the signal to introduce one is having to make similar flow changes in many places.

282.canonical: Keep programming logic out of the page in a Template View by delegating to a regular helper object, because embedded scriptlet logic makes pages messy and unmaintainable, blocks designers from editing them, and tends to mingle layers and duplicate domain logic; use a Transform View instead when the domain data is XML, and Two Step View only when screens share a common logical structure.

444.canonical: Treat trade-off analysis as a core architect skill applied as a repeatable, documented process — attending to the method used to reach the decision, not only the final answer — using the three steps of finding which parts are entangled, analyzing how they are coupled, then assessing the trade-offs by determining the impact of change on interdependent systems.

488.canonical: Design data encodings for both forward compatibility (old code can read data written by new code) and backward compatibility (new code can read data written by old code), because both are needed to roll out upgrades to different parts of a system independently; when older code reads, updates, and rewrites a record, preserve unknown fields, and remember data outlives code — it persists for years in its original encoding while application versions are replaced in minutes.

531.canonical: Do not build distributed coordination or consensus yourself — two-phase commit and consensus algorithms like Paxos are notoriously hard to implement correctly — but use a proven coordination service such as ZooKeeper, Consul, or etcd (which run a small fixed quorum voting among themselves while serving many clients) for small, slow-changing coordination data such as which node leads a partition, not for fast-changing application state; note that service discovery alone does not require consensus (DNS suffices).

550.canonical: Design applications around dataflow rather than treating the database as a passive variable: like a spreadsheet recalculating dependent cells when an input changes, view application code as a derivation function so that when a record changes, derived data (secondary indexes, full-text indexes, ML models, UI-shaped caches) is automatically updated — while recognizing this differs from ordinary asynchronous job execution because the order of state changes matters and losing a single message permanently desynchronizes the derived data.

659.canonical: Communicate and justify architecture in the business's own vocabulary by framing technical choices as real options sold to the business: design systems that defer decisions (deferral has value when more will be known later), map the real-options categories — defer, abandon, expand, contract — onto the design, and insist the business engage in the technical decisions, since IT alone cannot judge an option's value.

675.canonical: Invest in a well-tuned, fully automated build and deployment toolchain (CI/CD, configuration automation) to increase the system's rate of change — the toolchain is the software system's first derivative — rather than trying to anticipate changes through configuration, since coding the change yields simpler code plus version control and automated testing.

677.canonical: Treat quality as an enabler of speed rather than a tax on it: dispel the belief that speed opposes quality or that quality can be added later, because poor quality and developer fear slow delivery and cause code rot — instead build internal quality in from the start and automate to gain speed and quality together, judging test coverage by whether teams can change confidently rather than by line percentage.

714.canonical: Treat software-defined infrastructure as real software engineering, not mere hardware scripting or configuration: provisioning becomes a software problem essential for digital scalability but dangerous without code competence, so see through 'infrastructure as code' tools that are really configuration and instead apply a rigorous, fast-but-disciplined SDLC (disciplined development, automated testing, CI) to infrastructure.

716.canonical: Prefer interface and compatibility standards over product standards: interface standards (like TCP/IP and HTTP) enable interchangeability, independent evolution, and network effects, whereas product standards merely restrict choice — and shadow IT resists product-standard migration that brings cost without local benefit.

766.canonical: Treat the organization's ability to learn fast as its main competitive asset in a democratized-technology world and build internal skill to adopt genuinely modern products, paying 'tuition' only when it improves future decisions; consultants can boost this learning but cannot substitute for it, and as co-opetition they profit from the journey and will not make themselves unnecessary.

783.canonical: Find speed between activities rather than within them, because inactivity dominates elapsed time (often over 90 percent and sometimes exceeding 99 percent) and, by Little's Result and queuing theory, high utilization sharply increases wait times — so surface the often-invisible queues in calendars, steering meetings, inboxes, releases, and workflows and track wait time versus effort, since slow IT now means slow business.
